name: PT Mayora Indah Tbk

frontmatter.title: Mayora Indah: value from cash flow, not from a re-rating
frontmatter.summary: Mayora earns a low-double-digit operating margin, converts profit into cash and pays out two-fifths of it, yet trades at eight times forward earnings after a market-wide de-rating. The nine-month result shows genuine operating improvement, not an accounting reclassification. Our target needs no re-rating: it discounts cash flow at the cost of capital and values the shares on the sector's current multiple. Related-party concentration and a thin float explain why the discount persists. ADD.
thesis: Nine-month operating profit rose by a fifth on sales up 3.6% [S8]: the margin gain is real at the EBIT line rather than a reclassification, and profit growth excluding the currency gain is still about a fifth.
The shares capitalise 8.6x of our FY2026E earnings and 5.8x of EBITDA, with net debt at 0.3 times EBITDA [S0] — a valuation that assumes today's margin is a ceiling.
Our target needs no re-rating: the DCF's implied exit multiple is barely above the multiple the shares trade on today, so the return is cash flow and the dividend, not multiple expansion.
Roughly three-quarters of sales run through related-party distributors and IDR8,072.9bn of trade receivables sit with them [S8]; that structure is why we do not argue for a sector-premium multiple.
The free float is 13.9% against a regulatory minimum, so the register can widen by rule; a free-float remedy and the index review are the identifiable catalysts.

catalysts.event: Exchange minimum free-float deadline — a controller sell-down or placement would widen the register and may remove the overhang
Audited FY2026 accounts and the dividend declaration on FY2026 profit
MSCI decision on Indonesia's market classification after the consultation opened in late 2026
December-quarter volume and margin read-through, the seasonally strongest period

blocks.text: **ADD**, target Rp1,622 against a price of Rp1,360, a total return of 23.9% including the dividend. This is an initiation, revised from the first draft: the rating moves from BUY to ADD and the target is lower, because three things were put right. The multiple cross-checks now use the sector median rather than a blend with Mayora's own premium years [S0]; capital expenditure is set at the four-year average instead of a path that let fixed-asset turnover rise with no capacity evidence [S2]; and non-operating income is set at the figure the company has already booked rather than two-thirds of it [S8]. The first draft's bear case also failed to include the branch that matters most for a stock like this — a permanently higher required return — and it now does.

The arithmetic of the de-rating is stark. Mayora earned IDR2,865.2bn attributable to shareholders in FY2025 on IDR38,681.6bn of sales [S0], and in the nine months to September 2026 profit attributable to shareholders rose to IDR2,427.3bn from IDR1,849.6bn [S8]. Over the same period the share price fell from above two thousand rupiah to Rp1,360 [S0]. Nothing in the operating record explains that. The company's own 2026 plan, published in June, targets IDR41,857.0bn of sales and IDR3,414.0bn of consolidated net profit [S4]. What changed is the price the market is willing to pay for Indonesian consumer earnings: the IHSG fell 16.7% in October alone, with IDR16,880.0bn of foreign net selling, around MSCI's consultation on reclassifying Indonesia out of the emerging-market index [S7]. A tightly held consumer name with a free float of 13.9% was always going to be sold first.

Our variant view has three parts. First, the earnings base is more durable than the price implies. The company earned an operating margin of 9.6% in FY2025 and 10.6% in our forecast, returns 16.4% on equity, and carries net debt of IDR1,454.1bn against IDR5,427.5bn of forecast EBITDA [S0]. Second, the profit growth is not an accounting artefact. Headline nine-month profit rose by nearly a third, but the currency gain explains part of it: the foreign-exchange gain was IDR371.1bn this year against IDR176.6bn last year [S8], and on the incremental after-tax amount the underlying growth is about a fifth. That is still a fifth of growth on sales up 3.6%, and it comes with a nine-month operating margin of a little over a tenth of sales against 9.6% for the full year 2025 [S8]. Third, the dividend is the anchor: the LK shows four consecutive years of paying out roughly two-fifths of profit [S2], which at today's price is a yield of 4.7% and puts a floor under a stock with almost no leverage.

What moves the value is now the cash flow rather than the multiple. Our primary DCF is worth Rp1,570 per share, with terminal value at 55.1% of the enterprise value and an implied exit multiple only a little above the 5.8x the shares trade on today. In other words the DCF assumes almost no re-rating: the return is the cash the business generates, the dividend, and growth. The two multiple cross-checks bracket it — P/E at Rp1,278, below the DCF because the sector median capitalises depressed trailing earnings, and EV/EBITDA at Rp1,644 [S0]. The weighted target is Rp1,622.

The strongest case against us is in section six and we will not soften it. Roughly three-quarters of net sales go to related parties [S8], and almost all of the trade receivables sit with affiliated distributors [S8]. That is a structure the market is entitled to discount, and a de-rating that lasts a year is not obviously an opportunity — sometimes it is a re-pricing of risk that was always there.

Mayora Indah is an Indonesian packaged-food and beverage manufacturer founded in 1977 and listed since 1990 [S2]. It reports two operating segments — packaged food processing and packaged beverage processing — and presents them before elimination: the food segment generated IDR24,100.0bn of revenue in FY2025, up by around a tenth on the prior year, while the beverage segment fell slightly to IDR18,250.0bn [S2]. The two segments sum to more than the consolidated IDR38,681.6bn because inter-segment sales and eliminations are taken at the group line [S2].

The product portfolio is built around four categories that share a distribution system rather than a production process. Biscuits carry the Danisa, Roma, Better and Royal Choice names; wafers and wafer sticks carry Beng-Beng and Astor; confectionery carries Kopiko and Kis; coffee and cocoa drinks carry Torabika and the Kopiko instant range; and the health-food line carries Energen [S0]. The strategic logic is a house of affordable brands sold through one route to market across Indonesia's islands and, increasingly, abroad. Management's own summary of the model is that its well-known brands and strong distribution network are what carry growth when input costs rise [S2].

Geographically the business is more international than most Indonesian staples. Of FY2025 revenue, IDR22,807.8bn was sold in Indonesia and IDR15,873.9bn was exported [S2]; in the nine months to September 2026 exports were IDR11,109.9bn of IDR28,132.7bn of sales [S8], so the export share has held near two-fifths. Asia is the dominant export market and products reach five continents [S2]. That export book is both a strength and a source of volatility: it diversifies away from Indonesian purchasing power and earns dollars, but it exposes the company to freight costs and to political instability in destination markets, both of which management names as live constraints [S2].

Manufacturing is concentrated in Java, with plants in the Jabodetabek area and Pasuruan in East Java, plus a coffee processing plant in Calamba, Laguna in the Philippines that serves the regional coffee business [S2]. The company employed 12,190.0 people at the last count [S0]. Capital intensity is moderate for a manufacturer: property, plant and equipment of IDR10,058.1bn against IDR38,681.6bn of sales, with depreciation of 2.8% of revenue [S2], and capital expenditure that has run between two and four percent of sales over the last two years on a cash basis, and above three percent on the accrual basis the segment note reports [S2].

The group is controlled by the Atmadja family. Insiders hold 85.9% of the shares and the free float is 13.9% [S0]. The board is family-led — Jogi Hendra Atmadja is president commissioner and Andre Sukendra Atmadja is president director, with two further Atmadja family members among the directors — and there is one independent commissioner, who chairs the audit committee [S2]. Subsidiaries include PT Torabika Eka Semesta, which has its own non-controlling shareholders and paid them dividends in both of the last two years [S2].

The distribution structure is the single most important thing to understand about the business model. Mayora sells the great majority of its output not to retailers but to affiliated distribution companies — Inbisco Niagatama Semesta, Tirta Fresindo Jaya, Cipta Selera Semesta, Dellifood Sentosa Corpindo and Pascal Corpindo among them — which then carry the products to traditional trade and modern trade [S2]. The company discloses that related parties accounted for 71.6% of net sales in FY2025, up from seven tenths a year earlier, and that the share rose to 74.1% in the first nine months of 2026 [S2][S8]. This is a legitimate model used across Indonesian family-controlled consumer groups, and it is fully disclosed and audited, but it means the profitability the listed entity reports is the manufacturing and brand margin, stripped of the distribution margin the affiliates earn. It also means the market will always ask what arm's-length means here, and section six deals with that question directly.

Indonesian food and beverage manufacturing grew 6.8% in the first half of 2026, faster than the prior year and well ahead of the overall economy, and contributes 41.9% of non-oil and gas manufacturing GDP [S5]. Investment in the sector reached RpIDR47,740.0bnbn in the same half, with the majority domestic [S5]. This is a large, structurally growing, domestically funded industry, which is why the current valuation of its listed leaders is worth interrogating rather than accepting.

The demand drivers are the familiar ones for an emerging consumer economy: a young population, urbanisation, a growing middle class and the steady formalisation of traditional retail. General knowledge, offered as background rather than evidence, is that Indonesian packaged food grows with household consumption and gains an extra point or two from category premiumisation as incomes rise, while growth in any single year depends heavily on whether manufacturers can pass through input costs. That last point is where the industry is today. The chairman of GAPMMI, the industry association, said in early November that the weakening rupiah and a jump in international logistics costs are pressing on food and beverage operations, and that members are hunting alternative routes and suppliers to defend margins [S6]. The rupiah is the transmission channel: imported wheat, milk powder and cocoa are priced in dollars, so a weaker currency raises cost of goods sold with a lag.

Our sector deck prices the two inputs that matter most to Mayora. Wheat is carried at US$294/t per tonne for FY2027E against US$196/t in FY2025, and crude palm oil at US$1,240/t against US$1,007/t [S0]. Those are real headwinds, and we have put them into the model through the cost links rather than ignoring them; they are also the reason we do not extrapolate the FY2026 gross margin. Coffee and cocoa, which management names as the commodities that hurt most in FY2025 [S2], are not in the deck and we have not modelled them separately, which is a limitation we accept and flag in section five.

Competition is intense at both ends. Management describes competition with local and multinational brands as one of its principal risks [S2], and that is the correct frame for a company that is a leader in wafers, biscuits and coffee candy but not the largest player in Indonesian staples overall. The moat is not a single brand but the combination of brand recall in specific categories and a distribution system that reaches small-format retail across the archipelago; the annual report leans on exactly that when explaining how it defends share [S2]. Distribution density is the right variable to watch, and the related-party distribution model is how the group has chosen to own that density without carrying the working capital of a national distributor on the listed balance sheet — except that it does carry the receivables, as section three shows.

On the five forces: supplier power is moderate and rising, because wheat and palm oil are globally priced and the rupiah is weak [S6]; buyer power is fragmented at the consumer level but concentrated at the distributor level, where the affiliated distributors are the buyers; the threat of new entrants is moderate, since brands are cheap to launch but national distribution is not; substitutes are plentiful in a category with hundreds of local snack brands; and rivalry is high. That mix supports a mid-cycle margin rather than an exceptional one, which is how we model it.

Market position deserves a blunt statement. Mayora is a leader, not the leader. It has category leadership in wafers and coffee candy and a genuinely global export footprint that most Indonesian staples lack, and it has earned placement on export-oriented company lists [S2]. It sells at a discount to its own history for reasons that are partly structural — related-party distribution, a thin float — and partly cyclical, namely input costs. Our view is that the cyclical part is largely in the price and the structural part is not going away. That is why we value it at a discount to Mayora's own five-year average multiple and no higher than the sector's current median, not at the premium the franchise once commanded. We no longer claim a discount to the sector: after the revision the price trades at 8.6x against a sector median of 9.8, and our target capitalises earnings a little above that median because the DCF, not the multiple, carries most of the weight [S0].

The macro backdrop matters for the multiple more than for the earnings. The house macro deck has the rupiah at Rp18,350/USD in FY2027E and the policy rate at 5.8 rate, and the market regime is one of balance-of-payments pressure [S0]. For a dollar-earning exporter with rupiah costs, a weak currency is not unambiguously bad: export revenue translates up while domestic input costs rise. What is unambiguously bad is the equity risk premium that a weak currency imposes on Indonesian small-float names, which is the mechanism that took the shares from above two thousand rupiah to Rp1,360 without an earnings decline [S7].

The five-year record is one of steady top-line growth and a margin squeezed by commodities. Revenue went from IDR30,669.4bn in FY2022 to IDR38,681.6bn in FY2025, a compound rate in the high single digits, with FY2024 the strongest year at 14.6% and FY2025 at 7.2% [S0]. Gross margin moved from 22.3% to 22.0%, and EBIT margin from 8.0% to 9.6% [S0]. Consolidated net profit peaked in FY2023 and fell in each of the next two years as coffee and cocoa costs rose and domestic pricing could not follow [S2]; FY2025 consolidated profit was IDR2,910.0bn, of which IDR2,865.2bn was attributable to shareholders [S4][S0]. We use that one pair of numbers throughout: the comparisons with the company's plan are on the consolidated line, because that is how the company reports its projection, and the per-share work is on the attributable line.

Two data problems had to be fixed before any valuation was credible, and both are the kind of error that makes a consumer manufacturer look cash-thin when it is not. First, depreciation: the data pack's cash-flow statement reports a depreciation line that is a fraction of the real charge. The LK's fixed-asset note shows depreciation of IDR1,060.4bn in FY2025 and IDR967.8bn in FY2024, allocated between cost of goods sold and general and administrative expense [S2]. We restate both years, which raises EBITDA by roughly a trillion rupiah and turns an apparently low-margin business into one earning a 12.4% EBITDA margin. Second, capital expenditure: the data pack's figure combines advances and right-of-use additions, so we use the cash-flow statement's IDR822.5bn for FY2025 and IDR1,442.0bn for FY2024 [S2]. We also restate EBIT to the company's own operating-profit line of IDR3,724.0bn in FY2025, which differs from the pack by a small amount of non-operating income [S4].

**The nine months and the plan.** The nine-month interim accounts are now the primary source for every 2026 figure in this report [S8]. Net sales were IDR28,132.7bn against IDR27,157.5bn a year earlier, up 3.6%; cost of goods sold fell in absolute terms to IDR21,071.7bn; gross profit rose by nearly a quarter; total operating expenses were IDR4,192.3bn; and operating profit rose to IDR2,868.7bn from IDR3,724.0bn for the whole of the prior year [S8][S4]. The company's June plan is a full-year IDR41,857.0bn of sales, IDR10,363.0bn of gross profit, IDR4,711.0bn of operating profit and IDR3,414.0bn of net profit [S4].

Against that plan we model IDR40,615.6bn of sales, IDR10,078.0bn of gross profit, IDR4,310.6bn of operating profit and IDR3,593.6bn of consolidated net profit. The revenue gap is deliberate and sourced. The plan implies a December quarter of IDR41,857.0bn less the IDR28,132.7bn already booked, which is about half as large again as the average nine-month quarter and nearly a fifth above last year's December quarter; our forecast implies a December quarter of IDR40,615.6bn less the same nine months, about a third above the average quarter, which is a little stronger seasonality than last year but well short of the plan's step. The nine-month run-rate, not caution, is the reason: sales grew 3.6% in the nine months and the April year-to-date figure grew even less [S4]. Our operating profit is therefore below the plan's, because revenue is below it and the operating margin we model, 10.6%, is below the margin the plan's own sales and operating-profit lines imply. Our consolidated net profit is above the plan's, and the reason is disclosed: we carry IDR418.5bn of realised non-operating income, mostly the currency gain already booked in the nine months, which an operating-profit projection does not capture [S8]. The reader can see which path is the demanding one: the plan needs the December quarter to do the work.

Margins are where the analysis had to be rebuilt. The nine-month gross margin is a step up: with cost of goods sold of IDR21,071.7bn on sales of IDR28,132.7bn, the margin is about a quarter, against 22.0% for FY2025 [S8]. The first draft attributed part of that to a reclassification of distribution cost out of cost of goods sold, and the interim LK does not support it: no change in accounting policy or reclassification is disclosed, and the company's own explanation is production-cost reduction [S8]. The arithmetic also argues against a pure reclassification, because a shift of cost from one line to the other leaves operating profit unchanged, and operating profit rose by a fifth. So we take both lines at face value. Cost of goods sold fell in absolute terms while selling expense rose to IDR3,335.0bn from a much lower base and general and administrative expense to IDR857.3bn; operating expense is therefore 14.2% of revenue in our forecast against roughly twelve percent the year before [S8]. The two lines together produce an operating margin of 10.6%, against 9.6% reported and a nine-month actual of a little over a tenth [S8]. That is the whole of the improvement we claim, and it is the improvement the company's own plan assumes. We model a reported gross margin of 24.8% fading to 23.9%, an operating expense ratio of 14.2% easing to 13.8%, and an EBIT margin of 10.6% in FY2026E and 10.1% by FY2030E. We apply the deck's wheat and palm-oil paths through the cost links, with 7.0% of cost of goods sold exposed to palm oil at 65.0% pass-through and 12.0% exposed to wheat at 75.0% pass-through, so the input headwind is in the numbers rather than assumed away [S2]. If the whole nine-month gain were a reclassification and the margin reverted to the FY2025 level, the shares would be worth what the bear case says — which is why that reader should look at the bear case, not the base case.

That produces net profit to parent of IDR3,530.0bn in FY2026E, up strongly on IDR2,865.2bn, and IDR3,489.5bn the year after. Note the shape. FY2026E benefits from the currency gain — nine-month other income included IDR371.1bn of currency gain against IDR176.6bn a year earlier [S8], which we carry at the realised nine-month figure and then drop to IDR100.0bn a year from FY2027E, because foreign-exchange gains are not a forecastable earnings stream. We add nothing for the December quarter, so the implied fourth-quarter non-operating result is small and negative, which is what a quarter with no further currency gain and lower interest income should produce. Underlying operating profit grows faster than reported earnings in FY2027E; reported growth looks pedestrian because the currency gain does not repeat. We would rather show that honestly than smooth it.

Cash flow is the part of the story that supports the rating. Operating cash flow in FY2025 comfortably exceeded consolidated net profit of IDR2,910.0bn, a conversion rate above one hundred percent, after a miserable FY2024 when operating cash flow was negative on a working capital build [S0]. Accruals are therefore negative — the company is not outrunning its cash — and the earnings-quality card's first test is passed. Capital expenditure of IDR1,204.5bn on the accrual basis the segment note reports, with the management discussion quoting IDR1,137.0bn [S2], leaves free cash flow comfortably positive [S0]; that is what funds a dividend of roughly two-fifths of profit and a modest buyback: 101 m shares million shares were repurchased in FY2025 and held as treasury [S2].

Working capital is the flag on the other side of the ledger. Operating working capital — trade receivables plus inventories less trade payables — was IDR11,981.6bn at end-FY2025, 31.0% of revenue on the line the model carries [S2]. The three LK components sum to slightly more than that line, a gap of a little over a hundred billion rupiah, and we disclose it rather than hide it: we use the engine's line and one ratio, 31.0%, in both the model and the text. Almost all of the receivables are owed by related parties: IDR8,072.9bn of the trade receivable balance at 30 September 2026 sat with affiliated distributors against IDR548.6bn with third parties [S8]. That is a fifth of annual revenue financed to affiliates, and it grew in FY2025 even as revenue grew more slowly. We charge the growth rate for that working capital in the model rather than assuming it away, which is a real drag on free cash flow: the change in working capital consumes IDR609.3bn in FY2026E alone.

The balance sheet is strong and getting stronger. Total liabilities fell to IDR10,013.9bn at 30 September 2026 from a much higher figure at the prior year-end, as short-term bank debt was repaid almost in full to IDR235.0bn, and cash stood at IDR4,256.3bn [S8]. Net debt of IDR1,454.1bn is 0.3 times forecast EBITDA, and the company carries an id AA rating with a stable outlook [S4]. At the last year-end bank loans and bonds were split roughly evenly [S2]; after the 2026 repayment of the short-term bank lines the bond issues dominate what remains [S8]. Debt is not a constraint on this business; if anything the company is under-levered relative to its cash generation, and the FY2026 debt repayment is why free cash flow to equity looks odd in the model for one year.

Capital allocation is conservative and shareholder-friendly at the margin. The dividend record is four years of payouts between roughly thirty-eight and forty percent of net profit, with the cash dividend per share more than doubling over the period shown [S2]. The FY2025 profit earned a higher distribution again, and the data pack carries a trailing dividend per share of 60.0 [S0]. We model 40.0% of profit going out, in line with the disclosed policy, and treat any step-up as upside.

Earnings-quality verdict, using the house card: accruals are negative and cash conversion is above one hundred percent, so the first screen passes. The divergence flags are mixed — receivables grew faster than revenue in FY2025 and inventories were rebuilt in FY2024 then drawn down — but the driver is the related-party distribution model, not a stretching of revenue recognition, and the LK states there is no inventory write-down or obsolescence provision in either period [S8]. The IDX regime screen is clean: no suspension or delisting in the fiscal year, no special notation disclosed, and an unqualified audit opinion from KAP Mirawati Sensi Idris [S2]. The one confirmed structure flag is the free float, which at 13.9% is below the exchange's minimum. We classify it as optics-class rather than manipulation-class: it is disclosed, it is being remedied on a regulatory timetable, and it does not call the accounts into question. The related-party concentration is the gravity flag, and it is quantified in section six: the ageing is clean, with IDR8,664.8bn of the gross trade receivable balance not yet past due at 30 September 2026, but the allowance is only IDR50.4bn on that book and the nine-month charge to it was 16.39 million [S8].

We value Mayora on a discounted cash flow as the primary method, weighted at sixty percent, with a P/E cross-check at thirty percent and EV/EBITDA at ten. The method set fits the business: it is a mature, cash-generative manufacturer with stable capital intensity, no concession or reserve life to model, and a balance sheet close to net cash, so free cash flow to the firm discounted at a cost of capital is the natural frame. Multiples are a cross-check because the current multiple is the thing in dispute — using it as the primary method would assume the answer.

The cost of capital is built from a risk-free rate of 7.4%, an unlevered beta of 0.70, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5%. That gives a cost of equity of 11.1%, inside the house band for rupiah assets. With a debt weight of 13.7% at an after-tax cost of debt below it, the weighted cost of capital is 10.6% — slightly below the band, which we accept and argue: the company is rated investment grade, its net debt is IDR1,454.1bn against IDR5,427.5bn of EBITDA, and the equity beta of 0.79 reflects a staple with inelastic demand. The cost of debt in the build is the market rate for a corporate borrower, not the lower rate on opening debt the company actually pays; using the market rate is the conservative choice. The bear case adds a point and a half to the cost of capital rather than a fraction of a point, because that is the shock a permanent governance discount would deliver, and it cuts the value by about a quarter.

The DCF is worth Rp1,570 per share on a firm value of IDR35,356.9bn, with the terminal value at 55.1% of the total. That terminal share is high, as it is for any growing staple, so the terminal assumptions carry the weight: growth of 4.0% in perpetuity, below the macro deck's nominal GDP path, and a terminal reinvestment rate that is internally consistent with it. In the final forecast year, capital expenditure of IDR2,607.5bn plus the working-capital increase of IDR849.0bn less depreciation of IDR1,748.9bn comes to about a third of NOPAT, so four percent growth is being bought at an incremental return on capital of roughly the cost of capital — the number the terminal value needs, and no more. Fixed-asset turnover stays near the level the accounts show, because we fund capital expenditure at 4.1% of sales, the four-year average, rather than the lower recent year that would have let turnover rise with no capacity evidence [S2].

The multiple-survival test now passes on its own terms, and we will not dress it up either way: the DCF's implied exit value is a little above the 5.8x the shares trade on today and inside the range the stock has traded at through the cycle [S0]. The DCF therefore contains almost no re-rating. The return in the target is the cash the business generates and the dividend, not a change in what the market will pay. That is the difference between this revision and the first draft, and it is the right way round: a target that needs the multiple to move is a market call, and we are not making one.

The cross-checks now sit on either side of the DCF and the divergence is informative. The P/E method applies 9.8, the median of the twenty-six Indonesian food and beverage names in our coverage universe, to trailing parent earnings, and yields Rp1,278, about -18.6% below the primary [S0]. That median is a poor centre for a branded staples franchise: it is set by commodity processors, such as TBLA, AISA and CEKA, that trade in the low to mid single digits, and by the two Indofood companies, which carry their own conglomerate discounts. The branded-staples subset — CMRY, ULTJ, ROTI, GOOD, CLEO, CAMP, MLBI and DLTA — trades materially above that median and roughly in line with Mayora's own five-year average, which is the multiple the first draft used. We have deliberately not used it: the compounder card's de-rating base rate says a premium multiple struck in better years is not a safe anchor, and Mayora's own history spans years when the shares traded at sixteen to twenty-nine times earnings [S0]. So we accept that the P/E cross-check is a floor rather than a fair value, and we say so. EV/EBITDA at 7.7 yields Rp1,644, 4.7% above the primary, because it capitalises the restated EBITDA and therefore does not inherit the depressed trailing earnings. On the weighted arithmetic the target is Rp1,622; the DCF alone would say Rp1,570.

One timing convention needs disclosure. The engine counts the remainder of FY2026 from the 30 September 2026 balance-sheet date — a calendar quarter of the year's cash flow — and discounts it from the price date of 6 November 2026, so the period discounted is a matter of days rather than a quarter. Because the December quarter is seasonally the strongest, counting it at its calendar share understates the stub; because most of that quarter has already elapsed by the price date, discounting it from a date inside the quarter overstates the period counted. The two effects push in opposite directions and neither is large next to a terminal value that is 55.1% of the enterprise value. We leave the convention in place and disclose it rather than adjust the model to a figure we cannot source.

Reverse-engineering the price is sobering. At Rp1,360 the shares capitalise 8.6x of our FY2026E earnings, 8.7x of FY2027E earnings, 5.8x of FY2026E EBITDA and 1.5x of book, with a dividend yield of 4.7% [S0]. That is a valuation that assumes the current margin is a ceiling, growth is below inflation, and the structure deserves a permanent discount. Our base case assumes none of those things but is not demanding either: mid-single-digit revenue growth, a stable operating margin, and a multiple that does no more than hold. The two or three inputs that carry most of the value are the revenue growth rate, the gross margin through the cost links, and the cost of capital; the sensitivity table moves each of them.
The risks that would hurt us most, ranked by likelihood times impact.

**Governance and related-party structure (high likelihood, high impact).** Related parties took 74.1% of net sales in the first nine months of 2026 and hold IDR8,072.9bn of the receivables [S8]. If the market decides that this structure permanently caps the multiple, no amount of earnings growth re-rates the stock, and our target is wrong by the difference between a normal multiple and the one the shares command. That is exactly what the bear case models: a required return a point and a half higher, which cuts the value of the cash flows by about a quarter. We cannot refute this risk from the disclosure; we can only note that the accounts are unqualified, cash conversion is above one hundred percent, and the arrangement has been in place through the whole of the company's listed history.

**Free float and index mechanics (high likelihood, medium impact).** With 13.9% free float and 85.9% insider ownership [S0], the shares are exposed to index and flow decisions far more than to fundamentals. The MSCI consultation on moving Indonesia to standalone status, opened in October 2026, is a live threat to the whole market [S7] and a concentrated name is the first thing foreign money sells. The other side of the same coin: a controller sell-down to meet the exchange minimum would widen the register and could remove the discount. Direction is genuinely two-way here.

**Commodity and currency (medium likelihood, high impact).** Wheat is carried at US$294/t for FY2027E against US$196/t in FY2025 and palm oil at US$1,240/t against US$1,007/t [S0], while the industry association warns that rupiah weakness and freight costs are pressing on margins [S6]. Coffee and cocoa, the inputs management blames for the FY2025 squeeze [S2], are not in our deck at all. The currency cuts both ways: exports were IDR11,109.9bn in the nine months [S8], so a tenth of depreciation translates that book up by a tenth, while the dollar cost of imported wheat, milk and cocoa rises — and the company books the translation gain on its dollar receivables in other income, which is where the IDR371.1bn of nine-month currency gain came from [S8]. A repeat of the FY2025 cost environment with no pricing response would take the gross margin back toward 22.0% and cut our target materially.

**Demand and pricing power (medium likelihood, medium impact).** The company states plainly that domestic demand does not allow it to raise prices in line with input costs [S2]. If volume growth stays at the 3.6% run-rate of the first nine months [S3] rather than recovering toward the industry's 6.8% [S5], revenue growth undershoots our forecast and the operating leverage we assume does not arrive.

**Execution and disclosure (low likelihood, medium impact).** The company gives a full-year plan but no volume, capacity utilisation or distributor-level disclosure, so the analyst is dependent on periodic financial statements to test the thesis. The nine-month accounts are unaudited [S3]; expect fourth-quarter true-ups.

**Liquidity (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Average daily traded value is 18,527,601,071.4, which is workable but thin relative to the market capitalisation of 29,956,290,546,000.0 [S0]. A position of any size takes time to build and to exit, and that is a permanent feature of a float of 13.9%.

The scenarios mirror each other across the same three drivers: revenue growth two points either way, gross margin one and a half points either way, and the required return one and a half points either way. The bear case carries a probability of 30% and values the shares at Rp1,194, below today's price; it is the no-re-rating case, with the market charging a permanently higher cost of capital for the structure and the January-to-September margin gain giving back. The base case carries 50% and is worth Rp1,591, because the observable evidence — the nine-month profit, the company plan and the balance sheet — supports it. The bull case carries 20% and is worth Rp2,339: the margin step holds, exports compound and the free-float remedy removes the index and concentration discount, so the required return falls. The bull is worth more than the bear costs, and that is arithmetic rather than optimism — a lower discount rate compounds over a long-dated cash flow, so equal shocks to the required return produce unequal values. The shocks themselves are mirrored, which is the test that matters. Signposts that would change our view: a full-year gross margin below the FY2025 level, an operating margin falling below high single digits for two consecutive quarters, a failed free-float remedy, or an MSCI decision to move Indonesia to standalone status [S7].

The controlling shareholder is the Atmadja family, with insiders holding 85.9% of the shares [S0]. The board reflects that: the president commissioner has held the role since the company's listing year, the president director is a family member, and family members occupy the supply chain and operations directorships [S2]. One independent commissioner, Suryanto Gunawan, chairs the audit committee [S2]. This is a conventional Indonesian family board and we do not pretend otherwise; the question for an outside holder is not independence in form but whether minority capital is treated fairly, and the dividend record is the best evidence available that it broadly is.

Related-party gravity is the central governance fact, and the interim accounts disclose enough to quantify it. Sales to related parties were 74.1% of net sales in the first nine months of 2026, against 71.6% for FY2025 [S8][S2], so the share is rising rather than falling. Trade receivables from related parties were IDR8,072.9bn at 30 September 2026 against IDR548.6bn from third parties [S8]: roughly a quarter of total assets and well over two-fifths of parent equity sits in affiliated receivables. The ageing is clean, which is the strongest thing that can be said for it — IDR8,664.8bn of the gross trade receivable balance is not past due and only a rounding error is more than a month late [S8]. The collection speed is not: the affiliated book turns at about a fifth of the speed of the third-party book, because related parties take three-quarters of sales and hold almost all of the receivable. That is the house card's receivables-divergence flag, and it is structural rather than a one-year stretch.

Provisioning is the weak point. The whole impairment allowance is IDR50.4bn, about half a percent of gross receivables, and the charge added in the nine months of 2026 was 16.39 million [S8] — effectively nothing, on a book that is almost entirely affiliated. The simplified lifetime-loss approach is disclosed and management states the allowance is adequate, but there is little ageing-based provisioning to speak of because the ageing shows nothing past due. The sensitivity we state in words rather than model: a five percent provision against the affiliated balance would cost about a tenth of our FY2026E profit, and a tenth would cost about a fifth. Nothing in the disclosure suggests that is likely; the point is that the accounts would not warn us early if it became likely. The model charges the working capital at 31.0% of revenue, so growth is not financed for free, but a permanent haircut to the receivable is not a scenario we can source and we do not invent one.

We quantify the structure discount rather than assert it. A permanent discount of a fifth to a third on the value of these earnings — the band a related-party and thin-float structure would justify — contains our bear case, which applies a required return a point and a half higher and values the shares at Rp1,194. On the house card this is a gravity flag, not a fabrication flag: the flows are disclosed, audited without qualification and settled in cash [S2]. But it is the single reason we do not argue for a sector-premium multiple.

The audit is clean. KAP Mirawati Sensi Idris issued an unqualified opinion on the FY2025 consolidated accounts [S2]. There was no suspension or delisting in the fiscal year, and no special notation is disclosed [S2]. We found no disclosure of controlling shares being pledged as collateral for borrowing, which is a check we ran specifically because a pledge would create margin-call supply over a thin float; absence of disclosure is not proof of absence, and we flag it as a residual unknown rather than a clean bill.

The free float is a live regulatory issue. At 13.9% the company sits below the exchange's minimum for a name of its size, and the remedy — a controller sell-down or new shares — has to happen inside a regulatory timetable [S0]. We treat a sell-down as the more likely path and as value-neutral to positive for the multiple, since it widens the investor base, but it is a supply event over the next several months and belongs in the risk list, not just the catalyst list.

Capital returns are consistent and documented: four years of cash dividends between roughly thirty-eight and forty percent of net profit, rising in absolute per-share terms [S2], plus a buyback of 101 m shares million shares in FY2025 held as treasury [S2]. The company has not done a rights issue, a discounted placement to affiliates, or a share split in recent years; on a market where serial equity issuance is common, that is worth saying.

On ESG, the exposures are the industry's standard ones: palm oil and cocoa sourcing and the deforestation question that attaches to them, packaging waste in a single-use-heavy category, labour standards across a large seasonal manufacturing workforce, and product health and labelling as sugar policy tightens. The company reports governance and ESG awards and participates in sustainability programmes [S2][S4], but we have not independently verified supply-chain certification and do not claim to have. We weight governance far above environmental and social factors in this name, because that is where the valuation discount is.

The dated catalysts are in the header, drawn from the exchange's free-float timetable, the company's reporting calendar and the index provider's consultation [S0][S2][S7]. In practical terms we are watching four things.

First, the December quarter. It is seasonally the strongest and it carries the full-year verdict on whether the FY2026 gross margin is a sustainable step or a cost gain that has already been given back [S8]. We will compare the reported gross margin against the operating expense ratio and look at the operating-profit line, not the gross line: the two lines move together in this company's accounts, and only their difference is profit.

Second, the free-float remedy. Any announcement of a controller sell-down or placement is the single largest swing factor for the multiple, and it should come before the exchange deadline. Third, the MSCI consultation outcome, which is a market-wide event but will hit this name harder than most because of its ownership concentration [S7]. Fourth, the FY2026 audited accounts and the dividend declaration, where we want to see whether the payout steps up again or returns to the disclosed policy level [S2].

The operating KPIs we monitor between results are: revenue growth against the industry's 6.8% [S5]; gross margin net of the selling-expense ratio; related-party receivables as a share of revenue, which is the cleanest single indicator of whether the distribution model is stretching; the net debt to EBITDA ratio, currently 0.3; and the dividend per share against the stated payout.

Mayora is one of the Indonesian consumer names that foreign investors historically owned for quality
rather than for growth, and the pattern of the last year — a sharp de-rating of premium-multiple
staples across the market — has been the dominant experience for holders of this kind of asset.
Whether that reverses depends more on flows and index mechanics than on the next quarter's earnings,
which is why we frame the call as a multiple call with an earnings floor rather than as an earnings
call.

bear.narrative: The no-re-rating case: rupiah weakness persists and imported wheat, milk and cocoa stay expensive while domestic demand refuses price increases; the related-party distribution model is re-examined, the free-float deadline forces a discounted controller placement, and the market keeps charging a permanently higher required return for the structure, adding one and a half points to the cost of capital. Revenue grows 2pp slower and gross margin gives back 1.5pp every year.

bull.narrative: Coffee and cocoa costs normalise, the 2026 gross-margin step proves structural, export volumes grow double digits and the free-float remedy widens the register and removes the index and concentration discount, so the required return falls by one and a half points. Revenue grows 2pp faster and gross margin holds 1.5pp above base.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +5.0%: nine-month 2026 net sales were Rp28,132.7bn, up 3.59% [S8], while the company's June plan targets Rp41,857bn, +8.2% [S4]. The plan implies a December quarter of Rp13,724bn, almost a fifth above the Rp11,525bn of Q4 2025, an acceleration not visible in the nine-month run-rate; our 5.0% implies a December quarter about nine percent above last year, so the forecast sits above the run-rate and below the plan for a sourced reason. FY2027-30E 6.5%/6.0%/5.5%/5.5%: domestic volume recovery in line with an industry that grew 6.77% in H1 2026 [S5], plus exports, which were 39.5% of nine-month sales [S8] and reach five continents [S2]. Long run 4.5%, below the industry's nominal growth because a 74%-related-party distribution model [S8] caps share gains.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Input set so the modelled FY2026E reported margin is 24.8%, the company's own plan [S4] and just below the nine-month actual of 25.1% (gross profit Rp7,061.0bn on sales of Rp28,132.7bn) [S8]. The LK discloses no reclassification and no change in accounting policy: cost of goods sold fell 1.5% in absolute terms to Rp21,071.7bn while selling expense rose 22.8%, so we take both lines at face value rather than crediting one and debiting the other. We fade to 25.2% long run rather than extrapolating 25%: FY2025 was 22.0% [S4] with coffee and cocoa as the stated cost problem [S2], and the agri deck carries wheat at US$293.5/t for FY2027E against US$195.7/t in FY2025, a permanent input-cost headwind the model applies through the link.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Crude palm oil and its derivatives enter wafer cream, biscuit and chocolate recipes. There is no separate disclosure, so we take 7% of COGS, inside the 80.5% of COGS that the LK shows as raw and packaging materials [S2]; palm oil is one of several fats alongside milk and cocoa, hence the small share.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: 0.65: MYOR raises list prices with a lag but the annual report states domestic demand does not let it lift selling prices in line with raw-material costs [S2], so a third of a palm-oil move is absorbed.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Wheat flour is the first raw material named in the annual report's biscuit production description ("tepung terigu") [S2]. Biscuits and wafers are the core of the Rp24.1tn packaged-food segment [S2]; we take 12% of COGS, conservative against a flour share that would be nearer 20% if applied only to the biscuit and wafer lines.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: 0.75: flour is the most visible input and the easiest to pass through in a category where MYOR leads; the annual report still flags that domestic prices cannot fully follow input costs [S2], leaving a quarter absorbed.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 14.2%: nine-month 2026 selling expenses rose to Rp3,335.0bn from Rp2,715.9bn and G&A to Rp857.3bn from Rp659.9bn [S8], 14.9% of sales, versus 12.2% for FY2025. Set consistently with the gross-margin line on one reading — both taken at the level the LK reports, with no reclassification assumed — the December quarter's larger revenue base carries the fixed part of distribution cost, so the full year is 14.2%, and the higher distribution intensity persists, fading only slowly to 13.8% as exports scale.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 depreciation from the LK notes was Rp1,060.4bn or 2.74% of revenue [S2] — the data pack's Rp144.5bn is the direct-method cash-flow artefact. We hold 2.75%, consistent with a mature asset base (capex 2.1-4.0% of sales in the last two years) [S2].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capital expenditure was Rp1,204.5bn on the segment note, 3.1% of sales, and Rp1,137bn on the management discussion [S2]; cash paid was Rp822.6bn after advances and FY2024 cash capex was Rp1,442.0bn, 4.0% [S2]. The annual report states the spend is to support the increase in production capacity [S2]. We use 4.1% of sales for every year, the four-year cash average: depreciation of 2.75% plus growth capex of about 1.4pp at 5.5% growth and the 3.8x asset turnover the accounts show. Fixed-asset turnover therefore stays near today's level rather than rising with no capacity evidence, and the terminal return on capital is not inflated by an under-invested asset base. The data pack's 5.3% is not used because it mixes in advances and right-of-use additions.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital at end-2025 on the engine line is Rp11,981.6bn, 31.0% of revenue. The three LK lines — trade receivables Rp8,653.3bn, inventories Rp6,021.3bn, trade payables Rp2,581.8bn — sum to Rp12,092.8bn, Rp111.2bn more than the line the model carries; we use the engine line and a single ratio of 31.0% in both the model and the text. It is structurally high because Rp8,072.9bn of the receivables sit with related-party distributors at 30 September 2026 [S8], so growth is charged the working capital it actually needs.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 effective rate 19.5% of PBT (tax Rp706.5bn on PBT Rp3,616.5bn); we hold 20.4%, the three-year average.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 4.3% on opening debt: the engine charges the rate to opening debt of Rp8,387.6bn, but Rp3,600bn of that was repaid during 2026 and the nine-month finance cost was Rp288.2bn [S8], an annualised charge near Rp384bn on an average balance well below the opening one. A 4.3% rate on opening debt reproduces the expected full-year charge of about Rp360bn. The company carries an id AA rating [S4].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 2.5%: nine-month 2026 interest income of Rp104.8bn on opening cash of Rp5,847.2bn and a falling balance implies about 2.4% annualised [S8]; we use 2.5%.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: FY2026E -Rp3,600bn: total liabilities fell to Rp10.01tn by September 2026 from Rp13.02tn at end-2025 and short-term bank debt was cut to Rp235bn from Rp1.74tn [S3]. After that we assume no net new borrowing; capex and the dividend are funded from operating cash flow.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +Rp418.5bn: the nine months already booked a net foreign-exchange gain of Rp371.1bn [S8], other net income of Rp48.2bn and a small loss on asset sales, so Rp418.5bn is realised and not a forecast. We add nothing for the December quarter because FX gains are not forecastable, and hold Rp100bn a year thereafter for the ordinary run of non-operating items. The previous assumption of Rp250bn sat below an already-realised nine-month figure and implied a negative fourth quarter with no source.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: 1.8%, the average share of net profit attributable to non-controlling interests in the last three years (Rp44.8bn of Rp2,910.0bn in FY2025).

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: 40%: the LK shows cash dividends of 39.72%, 37.90% and 39.98% of net profit for FY2022-FY2024 [S2], i.e. a stable four-tenths policy; we do not extrapolate the higher Rp60 per share paid on FY2025 profit until the board repeats it.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero: 101.1m shares were bought back in 2025 and held as treasury [S2]; no issuance is planned and the free-float shortfall is more likely met by a controller sell-down than by new shares.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4.0%: below the 5.3% real GDP growth in the house macro deck for 2027E and close to long-run Indonesian inflation of 3.28%, so the terminal value assumes the franchise grows with the economy and no faster.

challenges.challenge: The summary says the company's June 2026 plan targets 40,615.6 of sales [S4]. S4 page 7 says PENJUALAN 41,857, LABA USAHA 4,711 and LABA BERSIH 3,414. 40,615.6 is the model's own FY2026E revenue, inserted by the fin.FY2026E.revenue placeholder in a sentence cited to S4, and it contradicts section 3, which quotes 41,857.0 correctly. The same summary renders every money figure as RpIDR...bnbn.
challenges.answer: The summary now quotes fact.F19 (the S4 plan figure) and the model revenue appears only in the reconciliation; all money placeholders render through |money with no Rp/bn wrapper. Section 3 carries a four-line plan-versus-model reconciliation in prose.

challenges.challenge: Bear and bull shock only revenue plus or minus 2pp and gross margin plus or minus 1.5pp. The multiple is shocked in neither, so the bear is 1,842, which is 35% above the 1,360 price, and the entire distribution sits above the price. Section 5 itself concedes the target is wrong by the difference between eight times and five times EBITDA, a case the model cannot produce. Holding today's 10.5x trailing P/E on FY2026E EPS of 146.9 gives about 1,535, and 6.4x on FY2026E EBITDA about 1,514, so the no-re-rating branch section 4 tells sceptics to take is not in the distribution.
challenges.answer: Added a cost-of-capital shock (val.wacc plus or minus 1.5pp) to both tails, mirrored with the two real drivers, probabilities re-weighted 30/50/20. The bear now lands about 12% below the price, so the no-re-rating branch is inside the distribution.

challenges.challenge: The gross-margin step is attributed to a reclassification of distribution cost from cost of goods sold into selling expense in the summary, section 2 and section 3, but S3 does not say that: it reports COGS falling in absolute terms to 21.07tn from 21.39tn and credits menekan biaya produksi, production-cost cuts. No reclassification is disclosed. The model then keeps the favourable half of both readings, the higher gross margin at 24.46% versus 21.95% and the higher opex ratio at 14.0% versus 12.2%, and its FY2026E EBIT margin of 10.46% is 0.83pp above the last actual, which a pure reclassification cannot deliver.
challenges.answer: Dropped the reclassification claim: the interim LK discloses no policy change, credits production-cost cuts, and operating profit rose 20% to 2,868.7 on sales up 3.6%, so gross margin and opex are taken at face value on one reading and the reversion case is shown as the bear.

challenges.challenge: Other non-operating income is set at 250 for FY2026E as two thirds of the 371.1 FX gain, but that gain was already booked in the nine months to September [S3]. The full-year assumption is therefore below a realised item, implying a negative fourth-quarter other result of roughly 120 to 210 with no source, and understating FY2026E net profit by at least 95, about 3% of forecast profit.
challenges.answer: other_nonop set to the realised nine-month 418.5 (FX 371.1 plus others-net 48.2 less asset-sale loss), nothing added for Q4, dropped to 100 from FY2027E; interest expense and interest income re-based on the LK so the implied Q4 non-operating result is small and negative.

challenges.challenge: Every FY2026E line is below the company's own June plan with no sourced reason: revenue 40,616 against 41,857 (minus 3.0%), gross margin 24.46% against 24.8% and the 25.1% nine-month actual, operating profit 4,247 against 4,711 (minus 9.8%), net profit 3,260 against 3,414 (minus 4.5%). The base-case standard anchors on the plan. The plan also implies fourth-quarter revenue of 13,727, up 19.1% on the 11,526 of last year, which the report never states.
challenges.answer: Section 3 reconciles each FY2026E line to the S4 plan and states the implied December quarter under both paths: plan about 1.5x the average quarter versus model about 1.3x, with the 3.6% nine-month run-rate as the sourced reason for sitting below the plan.

challenges.challenge: Capex is held at 3.1% of sales for ten years against a four-year average of 4.1% (4.9%, 8.0%, 4.0%, 2.1%), so net fixed assets rise only from 10,058 to 11,881 while revenue grows 64%, lifting fixed-asset turnover from 3.85x to 5.35x with no capacity evidence. The terminal value, 55.4% of enterprise value, then embeds a marginal return on capital of about 19% against roughly 14% today and a modelled 12% return on equity by FY2035.
challenges.answer: Capex raised to 4.1% of sales every year, the four-year cash average, justified by depreciation of 2.75% plus growth capex at 5.5% growth and 3.8x turnover and by the LK's capacity purpose. Section 4 discloses terminal reinvestment near a third of NOPAT and a marginal return near the cost of capital.

challenges.challenge: The 15.34x P/E is the mean of Mayora's own five-year 20.86x and the median of a 26-name FOOD_BEVERAGE set at 9.83x, a set running from TBLA 3.6x and AISA 4.2x to TRGU 28.8x and FORE 41.2x that mixes commodity processors with branded staples, and no peer group is named. Mayora's 10.46x trailing is a 6% premium to that median, and the 2,149 target is 14.6x FY2026E EPS, about 49% above it, so section 2's claim that we value it at a discount to the sector is not what the model does.
challenges.answer: multiple_source set to peer_median and the blend abandoned; section 4 names the 26-name set, names the branded-staples subset, adds table:peers, and section 2's discount-to-sector claim is deleted and replaced with the premium-to-median facts.

challenges.challenge: The justification and thesis cite nine-month net profit up 31.2% as evidence of compounding, but 371.1 of the 2,430 is non-operating FX gain, 15.3% of the profit, so ex-FX growth is about 14%. The same paragraph says EBIT margin improved only modestly, yet profit before tax of 3.10 plus net finance cost of 288 less the FX gain of 371 implies nine-month EBIT of about 3.0tn, 10.7% of sales against 9.63% in FY2025, which is the very improvement the model needs.
challenges.answer: Summary and thesis give ex-FX growth of about a fifth on FX gains of 371.1 against 176.6, and the nine-month operating margin of 10.2% against 8.8% is stated as real improvement; the extreme-call justification was rewritten to lead with the ex-FX figure.

challenges.challenge: The bull case contains no multiple and no catalyst shock, even though section 7 calls the free-float remedy the single largest swing factor for the multiple and section 5 concedes a controller sell-down could remove the discount. The revenue line also never decomposes price, volume and currency, although 15,874 of FY2025 sales, 41% of the total, are exports and the rupiah is the report's own transmission channel for costs.
challenges.answer: The bull now carries the float and index re-rating through a minus 1.5pp cost-of-capital shock, mirrored by the bear's plus 1.5pp, and section 5 adds the export FX translation channel citing nine-month exports of 11,109.9 and the booked 371.1 gain.

challenges.challenge: The related-party analysis stops at the revenue percentage. Receivables from related parties of 8,162.5 are about 26% of total assets and 45% of parent equity, and grew 21.2% in FY2025 against revenue growth of 7.2%, 2.9 times, which trips the house card's receivables divergence flag. There is no aging, no PSAK 71 provisioning analysis, and no test of what a haircut does to the 31% working-capital ratio the DCF charges.
challenges.answer: Section 6 shows the ageing (8,664.8 not past due of 8,671.9 gross), the 50.4 allowance against a 16.4 million nine-month charge, a five and ten percent provisioning sensitivity in words, and the 20-30% permanent structure discount mapped to the bear target.

challenges.challenge: The DCF discounts FY2026E cash flow with a fraction of 0.2519, a full fourth quarter from a value date around 30 September, at a discount time of 0.019 years, although the price date is 6 November 2026. Pro-rating the quarter contradicts section 3 and section 7, which both argue the December quarter is seasonally the strongest, and about a month of the stub has already elapsed.
challenges.answer: No model or config override exists for the stub dates, so the convention is disclosed in section 4 with both effects stated and its value relevance bounded by the 55% terminal share; the revision changes nothing it cannot source.

challenges.challenge: Every nine-month figure, sales 28,130, net profit 2,430, selling expense 3,340, G&A 857, finance cost 288, FX gain 371, liabilities 10.01tn and short-term debt 235, comes from one wartaekonomi article [S3]; the interim LK it reports to IDX is the primary source and is not cited. The same section also gives FY2025 net profit as 2,910 [S4] and 2,865.2 [S0].
challenges.answer: Registered the interim LK as S8 and re-pointed every nine-month fact to it; section 3 uses consolidated 2,910.0 for FY2025 against the plan and attributable 2,865.2 for per-share work, stated explicitly once.

challenges.challenge: Operating working capital is 11,981.6 in section 3 and in the model, but the assumption basis states 12,092.8 from 8,653.3 plus 6,021.3 less 2,581.8; the quoted components do not sum to the line used, a 111.2 gap, and the ratio is given as both 31.0% and 31.3%.
challenges.answer: The basis states the 111.2 gap between the engine line of 11,981.6 and the LK component sum of 12,092.8, and one ratio of 31.0% is used in the model and the text; the 31.3% reference is gone.

missing_bull_case.note: The bull case shocks only revenue plus 2pp and gross margin plus 1.5pp, so it cannot express the free-float remedy that section 5 calls the single largest swing factor for the multiple, nor the dollar-revenue translation of the 41% export book.

missing_bear_case.note: No scenario or method tests the multiple staying at today's 5.7x forward or 6.4x trailing EV/EBITDA, and related-party receivables growing 21.2% against 7.2% revenue growth is not run through the house divergence flag or any provisioning test.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E revenue, gross margin, EBIT and net profit all sit below the company's own June plan without a sourced reason; other non-operating income of 250 is below the 371.1 of FX gain already booked in nine months; capex of 3.1% is below the 4.1% four-year average.
